Repeatedly maximizing validation HR@10 creates selection optimism; ordinary confidence intervals around the winner do not remove it ([Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Recommended protocol: prespecify a small comparison—unchanged SASRec, SASRec plus fusion, SASRec with a fixed multi-negative objective, and that objective plus identical fusion. Fix seeds, checkpoint rules, fusion grid, trial count and compute limits; count checkpoint and weight searches as selection decisions. Multi-negative controls matter because loss changes alone can substantially improve SASRec ([gSASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07192)). Cache frozen component scores with user/candidate IDs and checkpoint provenance, then reuse them for the declared fusion grid; cheap scoring still increases overfitting opportunities if the grid expands adaptively.

For uncertainty, adapt [paired bootstrap resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250.pdf): independently resample 200 users with replacement within each dataset, using identical sampled user indices for every compared method. Compute each dataset’s mean hit difference, then average the four differences equally; repeat, e.g., 10,000 times for a percentile 95% interval. Report macro improvement, interval, per-dataset changes and discordant hit counts. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on frozen models and candidates; it excludes training-seed variability, negative-sampling variability and adaptive-selection bias. Keep all comparisons visible and label selected-winner intervals exploratory; use multiplicity adjustment for prespecified confirmatory comparisons.

Retain the pinned evaluator and untouched held-out evaluation. Describe results specifically as HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives: sampled rankings can reverse full-catalog comparisons ([Krichene–Rendle](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651)). Neither bootstrap precision nor a validation gain establishes full-catalog or online improvement.
